extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting §101 patent-eligibility analysis under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework, including considerations (improvement, particular machine, particular transformation, routine activity) and how to apply them to claim elements across technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to existing technology (Improvement consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of improvements is relevant to the eligibility analysis regardless of the technology of the claimed invention; an improvement in technology (not an improvement in an abstract idea itself) can show the claim is not directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that describe a specific way to solve a technological problem (e.g., particular rules to set morph weights for animation) and thereby 'improved [the] existing technological process' favor eligibility. This consideration applies across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). However, an improvement in the abstract idea itself (for example, an improved economic concept) is not an improvement in technology and does not favor eligibility. Examples of sufficient improvements: particular computerized methods of operating a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications), improved digital data compression methods (DDR Holdings; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), specific GUI configurations that improve accuracy (Trading Techs. v. CQG), improved hepatocyte preservation (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Anti-examples: commonplace business methods on a general purpose computer, using standard lab techniques, gathering/analyzing information by conventional techniques and merely displaying results, or selecting generic content/functions for existing hardware (various Affinity Labs, Symantec, Alice). See also MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer involvement must be particular and detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that the involvement of a computer assists in improving the technology, the claims must recite the details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding generic computer components to perform the method is not sufficient. A claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on a generic component or machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology. If applicant adds a generic computer or asserts the computer is 'specially programmed', the examiner should determine whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for mere-instructions guidance and case citations (Alice, In re Alappat, TLI, Eon, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more (Step 2B), examiners should consider whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful and important clue/investigative tool but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility. All claims must be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test; satisfying (or failing) the M-or-T test alone does not determine eligibility. Examiners may also evaluate related considerations (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use) when assessing whether a machine recited in a claim provides significantly more. See Bilski, McRO, DDR, and MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine recited with particular structure or detailed elements (e.g., specific antenna shapes/lengths, Fourdrinier machine structure) is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application. By contrast, a general purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional functions does not qualify as a particular machine. Mere recitation of concrete/tangible components is insufficient if they are conventional. See Mackay Radio & Tel. Co. v. RCA, Eibel Process, Ultramercial v. Hulu, TLI, Eon, Alappat, Bilski citations in MPEP § 2106.05(b)(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps rather than serving merely as an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. If the machine only functions as an obvious mechanism to allow a solution to be achieved more quickly or merely hosts the steps, it typically will not add significantly more (see CyberSource). Examiners should distinguish between machines that 'play a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed' versus machines that are only tools for execution. See MPEP § 2106.05(b)(II) and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine involvement must not be extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally/insignificantly (e.g., data gathering or field-of-use limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that merely contributes nominally (e.g., as a source of data or a field-of-use limitation) will not integrate a judicial exception or provide significantly more. Examiners should apply the insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations (MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h)) and review cases such as Bilski, Parker v. Flook, and CyberSource for guidance. Example: describing the Internet as a data source does not make fraud-detection steps tied to a particular machine. See MPEP § 2106.05(b)(III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a clue that the claim may integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or recite significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a particular, specifically-identified physical object or substance to a different state or thing (e.g., raw uncured synthetic rubber to precision-molded products; Tilghman v. Proctor) tends to favor eligibility. The M-or-T clue is not standalone; all claims must still be evaluated under Alice/Mayo. For data, mere manipulation of mathematical constructs is not an eligible transformation. See Bilski, Gottschalk v. Benson, CyberSource, Tilghman, Diamond v. Diehr, and MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for analyzing particular transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a transformation is recited, evaluate: (1) particularity/generality of the transformation, (2) how particular the recited article is, (3) the type/extent of change in state or thing, (4) the nature of the article transformed (physical vs intangible), and (5) whether the transformation is extra-solution or field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more particular transformation applied to specifically-identified articles that produces a new function/use is more likely to provide significantly more. Transformations that merely change location or are applied to generically recited articles likely do not provide significantly more. Transformations of physical/tangible objects favor eligibility over transformations of intangible concepts. Consider the Mayo example where body/blood administration was deemed only a field-of-use and insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(c) and cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether the additional claim element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry; if so, they do not amount to 'significantly more' and do not favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific limitations beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity and confine the claim to a particular useful application, they favor eligibility (e.g., DDR Holdings' dynamic hybrid webpage behavior modifying conventional hyperlink protocol). However, if additional elements are merely routine/conventional and recited at a high level of generality (e.g., measuring metabolite levels in Mayo), they do not provide an inventive concept. Examiners should note overlap between this consideration and improvement, mere-instructions, and insignificant extra-solution activity. Also remember novelty/obviousness inquiries are distinct from eligibility: an element known in the art can still be unconventional for eligibility purposes (e.g., Enfish). See MPEP § 2106.05(d) and case law (DDR, Mayo, Enfish, Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate related considerations: mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should evaluate whether claim elements amount to mere instructions to apply a judicial exception, represent insignificant extra-solution activity, or merely impose a field-of-use, as these considerations affect whether a claim integrates an exception or recites significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere instructions to apply an exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)) or insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)) typically do not confer eligibility. Field-of-use limitations that do not meaningfully limit execution of claimed steps likewise fail to provide significantly more (see Mayo and related discussion). These considerations are helpful when assessing particular machine/particular transformation/well-understood conventional activity questions.
